clue.text: Hardy work offered at Sothebys?

definitions.meaning: a poem by Thomas Hardy has this two-word title
Sotheby's is a London auction house where antique chairs and tables come under the hammer

explanation.surface: A Thomas Hardy manuscript is put up for sale at a famous auction house.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names both Hardy's poem and the antique pieces of household furnishing an auctioneer might sell; Sotheby's is a famous London saleroom.

clue.text: Her opus might be arranged for musician destroyed by women

indicators.note: arranging music suggests putting the letters of the two words into a new order

explanation.surface: A woman's composition could be scored for a musician torn apart by women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might be arranged' rearranges HEROPUS. The musician of Greek myth was torn to pieces by the Maenads, the frenzied female followers of Dionysus.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the lyre-player who went down to the underworld was later dismembered by Thracian Maenads.

clue.text: Some new-model Osiris in the Cyclades ()

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A newly modelled statue of the Egyptian god Osiris turns up on a Greek island.
explanation.definitionFit: The small island sacred to Apollo lies at the centre of the Cyclades group in the Aegean.

clue.text: Like P.D. James's causes

parts.note: P.D. James's first Dalgliesh-era novels include one titled with an adjective plus the word Causes; the clue asks for that adjective

explanation.surface: A question about the kind of causes in a crime writer's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: P.D. James wrote the detective novel Unnatural Causes (1967); the coroner's verdict phrase also fits a murder story.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes deaths not due to natural causes, as in the title of the 1967 detective novel.

clue.text: "Dick the shepherd, blew his" (Love's Labour's Lost)

definitions.text: "Dick the shepherd, blew his" (Love's Labour's Lost)

parts.words: "Dick the shepherd, blew his" (Love's Labour's Lost)
parts.note: the winter song closing Shakespeare's comedy has the cold shepherd warming a finger-tip by blowing on it; the clue asks for the missing word

explanation.surface: A line from the winter song at the end of Shakespeare's comedy, with its last word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The song 'When icicles hang by the wall' runs 'And Dick the shepherd blows his nail'; the clue quotes it with the final word left out.
explanation.definitionFit: The shepherd blows on his finger's horny tip to warm it in the frost, the word completing the quotation.

clue.text: No-account theatrical appearance of Kafka's work

indicators.note: No in front of a word means doing without it, so its letters are taken away

explanation.surface: A stage show with no story behind it is the way a Kafka book appears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No' takes A and C out of THEATRICAL, leaving THETRIAL. 'appearance of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz Kafka's novel about Josef K.'s arrest and prosecution is known in English by this title.

clue.text: Avuncular sort of narrator ()

parts.note: Joel Chandler Harris's storyteller of Br'er Rabbit tales is called Uncle, hence avuncular

explanation.surface: A kindly, uncle-like storyteller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Avuncular' (uncle-like) points to Uncle Remus, the narrator of Joel Chandler Harris's Br'er Rabbit stories.
explanation.definitionFit: The old storyteller of the plantation folk tales is known as Uncle, so he is literally an avuncular narrator.

clue.text: Tepid, like Paula Power?

definitions.meaning: Paula Power is the heroine of Hardy's A Laodicean; the Laodiceans of Revelation were neither hot nor cold

explanation.surface: Asking whether a woman called Paula Power is only half-hearted.
explanation.walkthrough: In Revelation 3 the church of Laodicea is rebuked for being neither hot nor cold, so a Laodicean is half-hearted; Hardy called Paula Power A Laodicean.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses mean half-hearted, neither hot nor cold: the water temperature and the indifferent Laodicean heroine.

clue.text: Concerning black French painter

parts.note: RE means concerning, as in a letter heading
noir is the French word for black

explanation.surface: A dark French artist is under discussion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French' turns 'black' into the French word, so the definition is just 'painter': Pierre-Auguste Renoir the Impressionist.
explanation.definitionFit: Pierre-Auguste of that surname was a leading Impressionist artist.

clue.text: Jilly Cooper book on Siena troubles recalls Chopin piece

parts.note: Polo is a 1991 novel by Jilly Cooper

indicators.note: troubles stirs up the city name so its letters are disturbed into another order

explanation.surface: A popular novel about troubled Siena brings to mind a piece of Chopin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'troubles' rearranges SIENA to NAISE after POLO; 'on' and 'recalls' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Chopin wrote several examples of this stately Polish dance in triple time for piano.

clue.text: Computer equipment apostrophized by Burns

definitions.meaning: the hand-held pointing device moved beside a keyboard
to apostrophize is to address directly; Burns's poem is addressed to a small field animal turned up by his plough

explanation.surface: A gadget for a PC was once addressed in verse by a Scottish poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Burns, Scotland's national poet, wrote 'To a Mouse', addressing the 'wee, sleekit, cow'rin, tim'rous beastie'.
explanation.definitionFit: The same word names a desktop pointing device and the field creature Burns addressed in his poem.

clue.text: "Kant, with his — morality, is a special target" (Colin Wilson)

definitions.text: "Kant, with his — morality, is a special target" (Colin Wilson)

parts.words: "Kant, with his — morality, is a special target" (Colin Wilson)
parts.note: a quotation with a word missing: Colin Wilson dismisses Kant's morality as a fake substitute

explanation.surface: A quotation from Colin Wilson attacking Kant's moral philosophy, with one word left blank.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing adjective means substitute or imitation, a German loanword fitting a jibe at a German philosopher's ethics.

clue.text: Magician shows how to thrive on nothing

indicators.note: on places the first piece ahead of the second, which follows it

parts.note: to prosper is to thrive
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A conjuror demonstrates how to do well from nothing at all.
explanation.walkthrough: The magician is the exiled duke of Shakespeare's The Tempest.
explanation.definitionFit: The exiled Duke of Milan in The Tempest commands spirits through his art and books.

clue.text: Extensive range used by B. Traven

definitions.meaning: a long chain of mountains with jagged peaks
B. Traven wrote The Treasure of the ... Madre

explanation.surface: A big mountain chain features in an elusive novelist's work.
explanation.walkthrough: B. Traven, the pseudonymous novelist, wrote The Treasure of the Sierra Madre, set in Mexico's mountains.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spanish word for a saw-toothed mountain chain names a range and appears in Traven's most famous title.

clue.text: The ranch made over for provincial boss

indicators.note: something made over is remodelled, so these letters are rebuilt in a fresh order

explanation.surface: A ranch is converted for a regional governor.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek-derived title denotes a ruler of a province or people, as under the Romans.

clue.text: Susan Coolidge explained what she did

definitions.text: Susan Coolidge explained what she did

parts.words: Susan Coolidge explained what she did
parts.note: Susan Coolidge wrote What Katy Did, so the 'she' is that book's heroine, named in full

explanation.surface: An author gives an account of what some woman did.
explanation.walkthrough: Susan Coolidge's children's classic is What Katy Did; its heroine's full name is the answer, so the author 'explained what she did'.
explanation.definitionFit: The eldest Carr daughter is the girl whose doings the American author's 1872 book describes.

clue.text: Youthful turncoat, supporter of Brutus

parts.note: young means youthful

indicators.note: turn tells us to turn the word over and rearrange its letters

explanation.surface: A young traitor backed Brutus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turncoat' splits as 'turn' (rearrange) and 'coat', giving CATO. Young Cato fights for Brutus at Philippi in Julius Caesar.
explanation.definitionFit: Cato the Younger's son appears in Shakespeare's Julius Caesar on Brutus's side at Philippi.

clue.text: Steward who told tale of a tell-tale

definitions.meaning: an officer who buys provisions for a college or inn of court

definitions.text: who told tale of a tell-tale
definitions.meaning: the Canterbury pilgrim whose story concerns Phoebus's crow, which reveals his wife's adultery

explanation.surface: A college servant told a story about an informer.
explanation.walkthrough: In Chaucer's Canterbury Tales this pilgrim tells of a white crow that tells Phoebus of his wife's infidelity and is turned black.
explanation.definitionFit: The title names a buyer of victuals for a college and Chaucer's pilgrim whose tale concerns the tattling crow.

clue.text: Racine's queen finds muse in a hot environment

indicators.note: an environment surrounds something, so A and H go round the muse

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hot on taps
Thalia is the Muse of comedy

explanation.surface: A French playwright's queen discovers her inspiration in a sweltering setting.
explanation.walkthrough: Racine's last tragedy is named after the biblical queen of Judah.
explanation.definitionFit: Racine's final tragedy (1691) takes its title from the usurping queen of Judah in the Book of Kings.

clue.text: Antiquary deemed lucky by R. P. Russ?

definitions.meaning: John ..., the 17th-century antiquary of Brief Lives

definitions.text: deemed lucky by R. P. Russ?
definitions.meaning: Patrick O'Brian, born Richard Patrick Russ, called his naval captain Lucky Jack

explanation.surface: An antiquarian scholar was thought fortunate by someone with initials.
explanation.walkthrough: Patrick O'Brian was born Richard Patrick Russ; his hero Captain Jack Aubrey is known in the navy as 'Lucky Jack'.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname belongs both to the author of Brief Lives and to O'Brian's sea captain nicknamed Lucky Jack.

clue.text: How could this German composer work without horns?

definitions.text: How could this German composer work without horns?

parts.words: How could this German composer work without horns?
parts.note: the composer's surname is also a Scots word for a cow without horns, so he could do without them

explanation.surface: A question whether a German composer could manage without the brass section.
explanation.walkthrough: Johann Nepomuk Hummel was an Austro-German composer; 'hummel' is also a Scots word for a hornless cow or stag.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of Beethoven's contemporary also names a beast that has no horns.

clue.text: Dead conducted Roman church

parts.note: the late means the dead
to run something is to conduct it

explanation.surface: A deceased man led services in a church in Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: St John Lateran is the cathedral of Rome, the Pope's own church.

clue.text: Beautiful Parricide later involved in unnecessary fuss?

definitions.meaning: ... Cenci, the Roman noblewoman executed for killing her father, subject of Shelley's The Cenci
the heroine of Shakespeare's Much Ado About Nothing

explanation.surface: A lovely murderess afterwards gets caught up in a needless commotion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unnecessary fuss' is Much Ado About Nothing; Beatrice Cenci killed her father in 1598, long after Shakespeare's Beatrice was imagined, but the name serves both.
explanation.definitionFit: The first name belongs to the Roman noblewoman executed for killing her father and to Benedick's sparring partner in Shakespeare's comedy.

clue.text: A Nickleby who is into moral philosophy ()

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the words that follow, running across the gap between them

explanation.surface: A member of a Dickens family who is keen on ethics.
explanation.walkthrough: Ralph Nickleby is Nicholas's grasping uncle in Dickens.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicholas's miserly uncle in the Dickens novel bears this first name.

clue.text: Like Laetitia Dale's self-centred husband

parts.note: Laetitia Dale marries Sir Willoughby Patterne, title figure of Meredith's novel about vanity

explanation.surface: Describing a woman's vain spouse.
explanation.walkthrough: In Meredith's The Egoist, Laetitia Dale finally accepts Sir Willoughby Patterne, the vain title character.
explanation.definitionFit: Meredith's novel takes its title from Sir Willoughby's self-absorption, which describes a person wrapped up in himself.

clue.text: Rebellious tribe, very cold, and supported by Northern Ireland

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits above the second, which holds it up

parts.note: ice means very cold, as in ice cold

explanation.surface: An insurgent tribe, freezing, gets help from Ulster.
explanation.walkthrough: The tribe led by Boudicca rose against Roman rule in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Boudicca's people in East Anglia revolted against the Romans in AD 60.

clue.text: An Eliot snob

parts.note: snob is an old word for a shoemaker; George Eliot's Middlemarch has a meditative shoemaker at the Tankard

explanation.surface: Someone in a George Eliot novel looks down on others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'snob' here is its old sense, a cobbler: Mr Limp is the shoemaker drinking at the Tankard in Middlemarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Middlemarch's cobbler at the Tankard bears this surname, and an archaic word for a cobbler is snob.

clue.text: Triumph in Wessex Cello Sonata

indicators.note: in says the answer sits within the words that follow, across the gap

explanation.surface: Success in a cello sonata from Hardy's country.
explanation.walkthrough: Wessex is Hardy's name for south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: To be outstanding or do supremely well is to triumph.

clue.text: Marryat's serviceman shows hesitation, attached to such a vessel?

parts.note: a private is an ordinary serviceman
er is a hesitation sound

explanation.surface: A Marryat sailor hesitates, serving aboard a certain kind of ship.
explanation.walkthrough: Captain Marryat wrote The Privateer's-Man, so his serviceman belongs to the kind of vessel the answer names; 'attached to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A privately owned armed ship licensed by government to attack enemy shipping is the vessel Marryat's hero serves on.

clue.text: Big Bang as described by Larkin

definitions.meaning: Philip Larkin's poem about a mining disaster has this title

explanation.surface: The origin of the universe as Philip Larkin pictured it.
explanation.walkthrough: Larkin's poem 'The Explosion' (in High Windows) describes a pit disaster.
explanation.definitionFit: A big bang is a blast, and Larkin's poem about a colliery disaster is titled with that word and its article.
